title: Search Open Technical Databases: Digital Certificates
shortTitle: Search Open Technical Databases: Digital Certificates
summary: The Transport Layer Security certificate that a service presents is public by design, and since certificate transparency logs became standard for publicly trusted authorities, every issued certificate is recorded in append-only logs that anyone can query. Each entry carries the subject organisation, the common name, often a list of extra hostnames in the subject alternative name field, plus validity dates and the issuing authority. An adversary queries those logs, or a commercial search interface built on top of them, to enumerate subdomains and internal-looking hostnames that the organisation never advertised. The data is historical, so expired entries still reveal names that existed years ago. Victim-side evidence is limited, because the queries go to the log operator rather than to the organisation, so the useful signals are search volume against your names and certificates for hostnames you did not create.

beginner.definition: A digital certificate is an electronic identity card for a website. It proves the site is really the one you asked for. Every certificate contains the organisation name and a list of addresses it covers. This technique means an attacker reads that public list.
beginner.whyItMatters: Certificates often list many host names that a company never publishes on its website. An attacker collects these names and finds systems you forgot about. Test servers and old portals are common discoveries. All of this is public, so you get no warning from your own systems. If you did not know a name existed, you cannot protect it.
howItWorks: The attacker looks up your organisation name in a public certificate search service.
The service returns every recorded certificate, including the host names each one covers.
The attacker collects names such as mail, test, or vpn from the certificate fields.
They repeat the search for older certificates to find names that still exist.
They check which of those names still answer on the public internet.
The resulting list then guides later scanning work or targeted phishing messages.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital where every visitor badge is printed with the departments that person may enter. Badges are handed out in a public room, and a notebook lists every badge ever printed. A stranger can read the notebook and learn the hospital layout. It shows a cancer ward, a records office, and a staff car park. They never enter the building, but they now know its shape. Certificates are those badges, and the public log is that notebook.
takeaways: Check what host names your certificates reveal before an attacker does it for you.
Old and expired certificates still leak names, so plan for a long memory.
Certificate logs are public, so treat every name in them as already known.

objectives: Explain what information a publicly trusted TLS certificate contains.
Describe how certificate transparency logs allow host name enumeration.
Explain why expired certificates still matter during reconnaissance.
Identify host naming habits that widen your exposed attack surface.
Outline how to monitor for new certificates that use your organisation name.
